prompt.context: An entrepreneur has recently bought a metal processing factory and wants you to design the supply chain system for the finished goods. You are his consultant.
prompt.question: How will you design the supply chain system for the finished goods? The client's specific objectives are: (1) focus only on outbound finished goods, (2) minimize cost, (3) ensure reliable delivery.

clarifying_info.q: How many products does the factory make?
clarifying_info.a: Focus on the outbound finished goods supply chain; product details are not the primary concern here.

clarifying_info.q: How many customers does the factory have?
clarifying_info.a: The factory has only one customer. All shipments go directly from the factory to that customer.

clarifying_info.q: Where is the factory and where is the customer located?
clarifying_info.a: The factory is in Chicago and the customer is in Denver. The distance between them is 1,000 miles.

clarifying_info.q: What modes of transportation are available?
clarifying_info.a: Various modes are possible (rail, air, road, etc.). For this case, settle on trucks.
The customer demand is 40 truck loads per week.

clarifying_info.q: What does the current transportation arrangement cost?
clarifying_info.a: The factory currently uses freight companies that charge $3 per mile per truck load (one-way charge).

clarifying_info.q: What are the costs if we lease our own trucks?
clarifying_info.a: Leasing cost: $1,750 per truck per month; Labor (driver salary): $0.50 per mile; Fuel: $0.30 per mile; Vehicle maintenance: $0.40 per mile; Loading/unloading: negligible; Insurance: covered by the lease provider. Assume 4 weeks per month. A truck can make only 2 round trips per week.

framework: Understand the supply chain scope: outbound finished goods only, single customer
Map the network: factory location (Chicago) vs. customer location (Denver), distance 1,000 miles
Assess demand: volume, frequency, seasonality — 40 truck loads/week
Evaluate transportation modes: rail, air, road (trucks); assess cost and reliability trade-offs
Analyze current vs. alternative transportation arrangements to minimize cost
Evaluate inventory and warehousing implications of the chosen transport option
Assess information flow and operational feasibility (driver management, maintenance, accounting)
Provide recommendation with quantified savings and risk mitigation

questions.prompt: Walk through your initial framework for designing this supply chain.
questions.guidance: A strong candidate covers: number of products, number of customers, demand profile, transportation modes, inventory, warehousing, factory and customer locations, and information flow. After structuring, the interviewer will narrow focus to transportation cost minimization.

questions.prompt: What modes of transportation could the client use, and which is most appropriate?
questions.guidance: Candidate should brainstorm rail, air, road (trucks), and intermodal options. For a 1,000-mile route with 40 truckloads/week of bulk metal goods, trucks are appropriate — good balance of cost, flexibility, and reliability. Interviewer will confirm: focus on trucks.

questions.prompt: The client currently uses freight companies at $3/mile per truck load (one-way). What is the current monthly transportation cost?
questions.guidance: Monthly cost = weekly loads × weeks/month × one-way distance × rate per mile.

math.setup: Monthly demand = 40 loads/week × 4 weeks = 160 loads. Freight companies charge one-way only. Cost = loads × distance × rate.

questions.prompt: The client is considering ways to reduce transportation cost. What options exist?
questions.guidance: Strong answers include: negotiate lower rates with current freight companies, seek alternative freight carriers, buy trucks outright, lease trucks, or relocate the plant closer to Denver. Interviewer will then focus the discussion on the leasing option.

questions.prompt: The client is considering leasing trucks. What information do you need to evaluate whether leasing is cheaper? Once you have that information, calculate the total monthly cost under the leasing option.
questions.guidance: Candidate should proactively ask for: lease cost per truck, driver labor cost per mile, fuel cost per mile, maintenance cost per mile, loading/unloading cost, insurance responsibility, truck capacity/utilization (trips per week). Then build up the full monthly cost: lease charges + labor + fuel + maintenance.

math.setup: Weekly demand = 40 loads. A truck makes 2 round trips/week, so trucks needed = 40 ÷ 2 = 20 trucks. Each round trip = 2,000 miles (Chicago→Denver→Chicago). Miles per truck per month = 2 round trips/week × 2,000 miles × 4 weeks = 16,000 miles/truck/month. Total fleet miles = 20 × 16,000 = 320,000 miles/month.
steps: Trucks needed: 40 loads/week ÷ 2 round trips/truck/week = 20 trucks
Miles per truck per month: 2 round trips × 2,000 miles × 4 weeks = 16,000 miles
Total fleet miles per month: 20 × 16,000 = 320,000 miles
Fuel cost: 320,000 × $0.25 = $80,000  [Note: casebook uses $0.25/mile for fuel in the calculation despite stating $0.30/mile]
math.answer: $403,000 per month under leasing vs. $480,000 under freight companies — saving $77,000/month

questions.prompt: What other ways can the client make more money or improve economics with this transportation system?
questions.guidance: A strong candidate identifies the empty-return leg: trucks return empty from Denver to Chicago. Opportunities include: (1) backhaul raw materials needed at the factory, (2) sell/lease unused truck capacity on the return leg to other shippers, (3) partner with a Denver-based company that ships goods to Chicago.

questions.prompt: What are the risks or negatives of the leasing option?
questions.guidance: Key risks: (1) driver management — HR burden, hiring, training, turnover; (2) accident/liability exposure on the road; (3) administrative complexity — tracking fuel, maintenance, and driver expenses requires accounting systems; (4) operational inflexibility if demand fluctuates (stuck with fixed fleet); (5) maintenance scheduling and downtime risk.

questions.prompt: Will the leasing system ensure reliable delivery?
questions.guidance: Candidate should address: dedicated fleet gives more control over scheduling vs. third-party freight; however, reliability depends on driver management, vehicle maintenance discipline, and contingency plans for breakdowns or accidents. Having 20 owned trucks provides redundancy. Risk mitigation could include a small buffer of contracted freight capacity for surge/emergency needs.

brainstorming.prompt: What other ways can the client make more money or improve economics with the owned/leased truck fleet?

categories.name: Backhaul utilization
ideas: Transport raw materials for the factory on the return leg from Denver to Chicago
Carry inbound supplies or parts needed at the plant

categories.name: Third-party revenue
ideas: Sell empty return capacity to other shippers as a freight broker
Partner with a Denver-based company that regularly ships to Chicago

categories.name: Cost reduction levers
ideas: Optimize routing to reduce deadhead miles
Implement preventive maintenance to reduce breakdowns and cost overruns

categories.name: Strategic options
ideas: Evaluate relocating the plant closer to Denver to reduce distance
Consolidate shipments to improve load factors if multiple customers are added

recommendation: Lease 20 trucks to handle the 40 truckload/week demand; this reduces monthly transportation cost from $480,000 to approximately $403,000, saving $77,000 per month (~16% cost reduction)
Pursue backhaul opportunities on return trips from Denver to Chicago to further improve economics
Establish robust driver management and preventive maintenance processes to ensure delivery reliability
risks: Administrative burden of tracking variable operating costs
Demand fluctuation risk with a fixed-size fleet
next_steps: Negotiate lease terms with providers and confirm insurance coverage details
Develop a hiring and training plan for 20 drivers
Identify backhaul opportunities — approach Chicago-area suppliers shipping to Denver
Set up accounting systems to track per-mile operating costs
Define KPIs for on-time delivery and cost per mile to monitor performance
